advances: Convex interpolation and the exact original x-mean suppress the masses of columns with large conditional-entropy deficits, even though the two outer masses need not be equal. This gives an absolute information-variance bound for the full width-three source class, including empty inner columns. It supplies a bounded source-information ingredient, not a general Weak Oertel conclusion.
author: research-agent
proof:
Let \(L\) and \(R\) be the smallest and largest occupied x-coordinates. Rank two makes \(X\) nonconstant, and strict positivity gives \(L<\mathbb EX<R\). Hence \(r:=R-L\) is either 2 or 3. If \(r=2\) and \(D\) is finite, translate x by \(-L\) and apply accepted fact dc73fc97e5139fdd. Its law \(\nu\) is exactly the pushforward of the present original law, its parameters \(\lambda,\beta\) are unchanged, and its integer denoted \(j\) is the present \(j_y\). The translated full supported mean is \((1,j_y)\); that fact gives the stronger bound \(\operatorname{Var}_\nu(\log\nu)<41\).

For the remaining cases, translate x by \(-L\). If the resulting x-mean is 2, then \(r=3\); reflect x by \(x\mapsto3-x\). Reflect y by \(y\mapsto-y\) if necessary. These transformations preserve completeness, rank, probabilities up to relabeling, both information variances, and the full supported integer-mean condition. The x-reflection replaces \(\lambda\) by \(-\lambda\), and the y-reflection replaces \((\beta,j_y)\) by \((-\beta,-j_y)\). Thus all subsequent notation refers to the transformed original law, with \(D\subseteq\{0,\ldots,r\}\times\mathbb Z\), both columns 0 and \(r\) occupied, \(\mathbb EX=1\), and \(\beta\ge0\). Its y-mean remains the integer \(j_y\), and \((1,j_y)\in D\).

For each occupied column \(i\), its integer section \(D_i:=\{y:(i,y)\in D\}\) is an interval by completeness. Finiteness of \(\mathcal Z\) forces its upper endpoint \(b_i\) to be a finite integer. If \(\beta=0\), it also forces every column to be finite. In general write \(D_i=\{b_i-k:0\le k<N_i\}\), where \(N_i\) is a positive integer or \(\infty\); the infinite alternative is possible only when \(\beta>0\). Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
s_{N_i}&=\sum_{0\le k<N_i}e^{-\beta k},\\
d_i&=\frac{\sum_{0\le k<N_i}k e^{-\beta k}}{s_{N_i}},\\
\mathcal Z_i&=e^{\beta b_i}s_{N_i},\\
\alpha_i&=\frac{e^{\lambda i}\mathcal Z_i}{\mathcal Z},\\
m_i&=b_i-d_i.
\end{aligned}
\]

Set \(\alpha_i=0\) for empty columns. Every entropy and every expression involving \(\log\alpha_i\) below is evaluated only on occupied columns. All sums containing column-conditional quantities run over occupied columns. Write \(s_i=s_{N_i}\), and let \(H_i\) be the natural-log entropy of the original conditional law given \(X=i\). Its geometric form gives \(H_i=\log s_i+\beta d_i\). Both original mean equations are retained exactly:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\alpha_0=\alpha_2,& r=2,\\
\alpha_0=\alpha_2+2\alpha_3,& r=3,
\end{array}
\qquad
\sum_i\alpha_i(b_i-d_i)=j_y\in\mathbb Z,
\qquad (1,j_y)\in D.
\]

For \(\beta>0\) and finite \(N\), the finite geometric sum and its logarithmic derivative give \(s_N=(1-e^{-N\beta})/(1-e^{-\beta})\) and \(d_N=(e^\beta-1)^{-1}-N/(e^{N\beta}-1)\). For \(N=\infty\), the convergent geometric series gives \(s_\infty=(1-e^{-\beta})^{-1}\) and \(d_\infty=(e^\beta-1)^{-1}\). Thus \(0\le\beta d_i\le\beta/(e^\beta-1)\le1\). At \(\beta=0\), \(s_N=N\) and \(\beta d_i=0\), so the same bound holds. Differentiating the geometric sums twice also gives, for finite \(N_i\) and \(\beta>0\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta^2\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=i)
&=\beta^2\left\{\frac{e^{-\beta}}{(1-e^{-\beta})^2}
-\frac{N_i^2e^{-N_i\beta}}{(1-e^{-N_i\beta})^2}\right\}\\
&\le\left(\frac{\beta}{2\sinh(\beta/2)}\right)^2\le1.
\end{aligned}
\]

For an infinite column the same formula holds with the subtracted term omitted, directly from the convergent geometric series. At \(\beta=0\) the conditional log probability is constant, so its information variance is zero. These calculations show that all occupied conditional information variances are at most 1, and the conditional log probabilities have finite second moments.

We next bound the between-column entropy variance. For \(p\in(0,1]\), writing \(t=-\log p\) and maximizing \(t^2e^{-t}\) gives \(p(\log p)^2\le4/e^2\). There are at most four occupied columns, whence \(\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(\log\alpha_i)\le16/e^2<3\). Here and below, \(e>8/3\) follows by retaining the first four terms of its positive power series; in particular \(\log6<2\).

If \(\beta\ge1\), each \(H_i\) is nonnegative and \(H_i\le-\log(1-e^{-1})+1<2\). Consequently \(\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(H_i)\le\sum_i\alpha_i(H_i-1)^2\le1\). This already suffices for the final bound.

It remains to consider \(0\le\beta\le1\). Let \(M=\max_i N_i\), allowing \(M=\infty\), and let \(S=\max_i s_i\). If \(M\le3\), then \(0\le H_i\le\log3+1<3\), so \(\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(H_i)<9\). This case allows any empty inner column and also suffices for the final bound.

Suppose now that \(M\ge4\) or \(M=\infty\). Every interior column is occupied, and

\[
s_i\ge S/6\qquad(0<i<r).
\]

To prove this, first let \(M\) be finite and choose a column \(k\) of size \(M\). For an interior index \(i\ne k\), choose an occupied outer column \(\ell\) on the other side of \(i\) from \(k\), so \(\min\{k,\ell\}<i<\max\{k,\ell\}\). Interpolating the entire integer interval in column \(k\) with one point of column \(\ell\) produces, in the real section at \(i\), an interval of length at least \((M-1)/3\), since the coefficient of column \(k\) is at least \(1/3\). An interval of length at least 1 contains an integer; completeness puts its integers in \(D_i\). Its integer count is at least \(\lfloor(M-1)/3\rfloor\). For \(4\le M\le6\), this count is at least \(1\ge M/6\). For \(M\ge6\), it is at least \((M-3)/3\ge M/6\). If \(i=k\), the same size bound is immediate. Hence \(N_i\ge M/6\) at every interior index. The sequence \(s_N/N\) is nonincreasing because it averages the first \(N\) terms of a positive nonincreasing sequence. Together with monotonicity of \(s_N\), this implies \(s_i\ge s_M/6=S/6\). If \(M=\infty\), use arbitrarily long finite intervals in a column with infinite size in the same interpolation argument. Every interior column then has infinite size and \(s_i=s_\infty=S\). This proves the displayed comparison in all cases.

Completeness also gives the upper-endpoint interpolation inequality. For occupied columns \(p,i,q\) with \(p<i<q\), put \(\theta=(i-p)/(q-p)\in(0,1)\). Then \(b_i\ge\lfloor(1-\theta)b_p+\theta b_q\rfloor\ge(1-\theta)b_p+\theta b_q-1\). Indeed, convexity puts the interpolated endpoint in the real section at \(i\); that section also contains \(b_i\), and completeness would include the integer floor between them if that floor exceeded \(b_i\). Cancellation of the original \(\lambda\) and \(\mathcal Z\) factors therefore yields

\[
\alpha_i\ge e^{-1}
\frac{s_i}{s_p^{1-\theta}s_q^\theta}
\alpha_p^{1-\theta}\alpha_q^\theta
\qquad(p<i<q,\ 0\le\beta\le1).
\]

For each occupied column set \(t_i=\log(S/s_i)\ge0\). The interior comparison proves \(t_i\le\log6\) for \(0<i<r\).

For \(r=3\), set \(a=\alpha_0\). The exact x-mean gives \(a=\alpha_2+2\alpha_3\); thus either \(\alpha_2\ge a/2\) or \(\alpha_3\ge a/4\). Choose the corresponding \(k\in\{2,3\}\) and apply the preceding interpolation inequality at \(i=1\) between occupied columns 0 and \(k\), which satisfy \(0<1<k\). Since \(s_1\ge S/6\), \(s_k\le S\), and \(1-1/k\ge1/2\), it gives

\[
\alpha_1\ge\frac{1}{6e}e^{(1-1/k)t_0}
a^{1-1/k}\alpha_k^{1/k}
\ge\frac{a}{12e}e^{t_0/2}.
\]

The last inequality uses \(2^{1/2}\le2\) in the first alternative and \(4^{1/3}\le2\) in the second. Since \(\alpha_1\le1\), this proves \(\alpha_0\le12e e^{-t_0/2}\). At \(i=2\), interpolate between occupied columns 0 and 3, which satisfy \(0<2<3\). Here \(\theta=2/3\), \(s_2\ge S/6\), and the exact mean gives \(\alpha_0\ge2\alpha_3\). Thus

\[
\alpha_2\ge\frac1{6e}e^{2t_3/3}
\alpha_0^{1/3}\alpha_3^{2/3}
\ge\frac1{6e}e^{2t_3/3}\alpha_3,
\qquad
\alpha_3\le6e e^{-2t_3/3}.
\]

For \(c>0\), elementary differentiation gives \(\max_{t\ge0}t^2e^{-ct}=4/(c^2e^2)\). The endpoint bounds therefore imply \(\alpha_0t_0^2\le192/e\) and \(\alpha_3t_3^2\le54/e\). The two interior columns contribute at most \((\log6)^2\), so

\[
\sum_i\alpha_i t_i^2\le\frac{246}{e}+(\log6)^2
<\frac{369}{4}+4=\frac{385}{4}<97.
\]

For \(r=2\), the exact mean instead gives \(\alpha_0=\alpha_2=a\). Interpolation at \(i=1\) between occupied columns 0 and 2, with \(0<1<2\), gives \(\alpha_1\ge(6e)^{-1}a e^{t_0/2}\) because \(s_2\le S\), and also \(\alpha_1\ge(6e)^{-1}a e^{t_2/2}\) because \(s_0\le S\). Hence \(\alpha_i\le6e e^{-t_i/2}\) for each endpoint \(i\in\{0,2\}\). Their combined contribution is at most \(192/e<246/e\), and the one interior column contributes at most \((\log6)^2\). Thus the same strict bound \(\sum_i\alpha_i t_i^2<97\) holds. This argument covers the infinite-support width-two case without applying the finite-support predecessor beyond its hypotheses.

Using \(H_i=\log S-t_i+\beta d_i\), \(0\le\beta d_i\le1\), and \((u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2\), we now obtain

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(H_i)
\le\sum_i\alpha_i(H_i-\log S)^2
\le2\sum_i\alpha_i t_i^2+2<196.
\]

Combining this with the small-column and large-\(\beta\) cases proves \(\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(H_i)<196\) uniformly. Centering the two random variables and using the same quadratic inequality gives

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(\log\alpha_i-H_i)
\le2\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(\log\alpha_i)
+2\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(H_i)<6+392=398.
\]

The conditional expectation of the original log probability is exactly \(\mathbb E[\log\nu(X,Y)\mid X=i]=\log\alpha_i-H_i\). The conditional variance is \(\beta^2\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=i)\le1\). Total variance therefore yields

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\nu(\log\nu)
=\sum_i\alpha_i\beta^2\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=i)
+\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(\log\alpha_i-H_i)<399<400.
\]

All interpolations and mass comparisons used the same original law throughout. The supported full y-mean was explicitly retained, although the estimates in fact require only the stated x-mean and completeness once their column conditions are established.

u(x,y)=e^{\lambda x+ eta y}/\mathcal Z\). Suppose the full mean exists and satisfies \(\mathbb E_
u(X,Y)=(j,j_y)\), where \(j\in\{1,2\}\), \(j_y\in\mathbb Z\), and \((j,j_y)\in D\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}_

In particular, this holds for every finite \(D\) in the stated source class and every original tilt satisfying the full supported integer-mean condition. No log-concavity assumption is imposed on the projected column masses. The proof also covers infinite \(D\) under the explicitly stated finite-partition and existing-full-mean hypotheses.
